title: Ibrahim's du'a
hook: make me and my children keep the prayer, and accept my prayer (14:40)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Adam's du'a, rabbana zalamna anfusana, and your line, we wronged ourselves. Today, a prayer from a man at the other end of a long life.

Ibrahim has done almost everything a person of faith could do. He broke the idols. He walked out of the fire. He left his wife and baby in an empty valley on Allah's word. With his son Isma'il, he raised the walls of the Ka'bah, stone by stone. If anyone had earned the right to feel sure of himself, it's him. And at the end of his prayer in surah fourteen, he still asks to be kept, and to be accepted.

Surah Ibrahim, verse forty, in Pickthall's translation: "My Lord! Make me to establish proper worship, and some of my posterity (also); our Lord! and accept the prayer." Two requests. The first: make me keep up the prayer, me and my children after me. Not make me rich, not make me remembered. Keep me praying, and keep them praying. He asks for himself first. Even Ibrahim doesn't assume he'll stay steady on his own. The second is today's line: wa taqabbal du'a', and accept my prayer. Asking isn't the end of it. He asks for the asking to be received. In the next verse he widens the circle: our Lord, forgive me, and my parents, and the believers, on the day the reckoning is set up. Here's the scholar's thread. He says the same kind of thing in al-Baqarah, verse one twenty-seven, while the walls of the Ka'bah are going up: our Lord, accept from us. Commentators record that an early pious man, Wuhayb ibn al-Ward, wept when he recited it: the Friend of the Merciful is building Allah's own House, and he's afraid it won't be accepted. In both places, Ibrahim doesn't treat a good deed as finished just because it's done. Some Muslims recite these verses, fourteen forty and forty-one, in the last sitting of their prayer, so the prayer ends asking for itself to be accepted.

Bring your family to mind one by one, parents, children, siblings, a partner, and picture each in a quiet moment of their own, praying, pausing, or looking for meaning in their way. If you pray, ask for each by name, as Ibrahim did, that they keep their prayer, then add his last words: and accept my prayer. If you don't, simply wish each of them steadiness.
Ibrahim's du'a. Make me and my children keep the prayer, and accept my prayer: the builder of the Ka'bah, still asking to be accepted. Today's word.
Your line: accept my prayer. A good deed still asks to be received. Until tomorrow.

fork.setup: you've just finished building the Ka'bah with your son, at Allah's command. what do you pray?
options: make it the greatest house on earth.
fork.reveal: Ibrahim and Isma'il ask for acceptance (2:127), and commentators record that an early pious man wept at it.

original.note: Arabic, 14:40: our Lord, and accept my prayer.

trapdoor: what you thought: Ibrahim prayed for his children.
what it means: he prayed to keep the prayer himself, then for his children, and asked for the prayer itself to be accepted.
what a scholar hears: taqabbal echoes 2:127; Ibn Kathir records Wuhayb ibn al-Ward weeping that the Friend of the Merciful feared rejection.

chat.says: Ibrahim built the Ka'bah. Why would he still ask for his prayer to be accepted?
options: He didn't treat a good deed as finished; he asked: accept my prayer, accept from us.
He had done something wrong while building it, and wanted it forgiven.
He wasn't asking; he was reminding God of everything he had earned.
chat.meaning: 14:40 ends: and accept the prayer. At the Ka'bah, 2:127: our Lord, accept from us.

Ka'bah.meaning: the House in Mecca that Ibrahim and Isma'il raised

Isma'il.meaning: Ibrahim's son, who helped raise the Ka'bah

Wuhayb ibn al-Ward.meaning: an early pious man who wept at 2:127
